title_original: Pierrot Men Captures Madagascar’s Post-Independence History
excerpt_original: A sprawling retrospective of the documentary photographer's work provides a tender view on Madagascar's post-independence history

blocks.text: A sprawling retrospective of the documentary photographer’s work takes a tender view of violent times

Pierrot Men’s Portraits of Insurgents (2008–13), nine images of which are included in this sprawling exhibition showcasing the work of the pioneering, wide-ranging Malagasy documentary photographer, honours the legacy of the 1947 anti-colonial uprising and Madagascar’s independence struggle against its then colonial rulers, France. A 2009 work from the Fianarantsoa series (1989–2015) – named for the place where Men has lived and worked for decades – shows a pensive-looking elderly man wearing a fedora, his hands supporting his chin, seemingly lost in recalling the events he participated in. In a 2010 work from the same grouping, a different fedora-wearing older man salutes a Malagasy flag during a commemoration of the uprising. These images, in equal parts, tell the story of the East African nation and perhaps allude to Men’s own life, and his affinity for his birth country and its history. They’re part, here, of a mixture of about 300 black-and-white and 75 colour images – among other elements – covering people from all walks of life, landscapes, monuments, cultural and religious events, and the photographer’s life as a family man.

Work from the 2016 Procession series brings to the fore Men’s interest in religion, faith and community. In Ankaramalaza (2016) hundreds of people are seen walking on a street during the 150th anniversary of the Malagasy Lutheran Church, a towering tree in the background and clouds overhead. Soatanana (2012), from a series begun in the 1980s, shows a group of people belonging to the Fifohazana , a Christian Revival Church, some wearing fedoras, others wearing handwoven hats and a few toting umbrellas, headed to a Sunday church service. There are, elsewhere, a not insignificant amount of sensitive images of funerals, graves and cemeteries. The photographer has had his own losses to deal with, as seen in images such as Autoportrait, Fianarantsoa. Matsiatra Ambony (1995), where Men’s shadow lays over his son’s grave, which is decorated with flowers he’d placed there. Lucette Men avec ses deux fils, Meddy et Florian. Fianarantsoa. Matsiatra Ambony is a 1994 image of Pierrot’s second wife and their children heading to a cemetery to place flowers on the grave of his first wife, Yvonne, who died during childbirth.

blocks.caption: Autoportrait, Fianarantsoa. Matsiatra Ambony , 1995, b/w photograph. Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: Nearby is a painting by Men of Yvonne: Portrait d’Yvonne Men, femme de Pierrot Men (1981), which shows her with short hair pulled up to her neck, parted in the middle at the top, wearing what appears to be a winter jacket and directing a soft, loving stare at someone out of frame. The painting is one of about a dozen colourful portrait paintings in the show, providing visitors with the rarely mentioned information that this was Men’s first medium before his turn to photography, indirectly explaining the painting-like and emotional depth that he brings to his circa five decades of photographic work. Among his broad range of subjects, Men’s images provide an unvarnished account of Madagascar post-independence history and the country’s transformation in the decades since through thoughtful and humanised documentary photography. While a well-curated tribute to the status of its subject, his work and his country’s multifaceted past and present, in light of recent social and political events in the country – protests, shifts in government – this show could also be considered a potent reminder of what’s at stake.
Pierrot Men, FOFON’AINA. WINDS OF LIFE. VENTS DE VIE , is on view at Hakanto Contemporary, Antananarivo through 14 February
